final_proof:
Work in ZF; no form of the axiom of choice will be used. We call a set countable if it injects into ω (equivalently here, if it is finite or equipotent with a subset of ω).

We first record the standard comparison fact for well-orders, including the part of its proof that will be needed below. For a well-order (X,<), write X_{<x}={z∈X:z<x}. A well-order is not isomorphic to any of its proper initial segments. Indeed, if f:X→X_{<a} were an order isomorphism, choose the least x for which f(x)≠x; such an x exists because the range omits a. If f(x)<x, then f(x) is fixed by the minimality of x, and injectivity applied to f(f(x))=f(x) gives f(x)=x, a contradiction. If x<f(x), then x<f(x)<a, so x is in the range of f. Say f(z)=x. Since f(z)<f(x), we have z<x, whence f(z)=z by minimality; this again gives z=x, a contradiction.

Now let (X,<) and (Y,◁) be any two well-orders. Relate x∈X to y∈Y when X_{<x} and Y_{<y} are order-isomorphic. For a fixed x there is at most one such y, and conversely: two different predecessor segments of one well-order cannot be isomorphic, by the preceding paragraph. The resulting correspondence is an order isomorphism between an initial segment I of X and an initial segment J of Y. If both I and J were proper, and x₀ and y₀ were the least elements outside them, that correspondence would be an isomorphism X_{<x₀}=I→J=Y_{<y₀}; hence x₀ would correspond to y₀, contrary to their exclusion. Thus at least one of I,J is the whole set. It follows that exactly one of the following holds: X and Y are isomorphic; X is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of Y; or Y is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of X. This is the well-order comparison theorem, proved without choice. (The assertion above that I and J are initial and that the correspondence preserves order follows by restricting an isomorphism between predecessor segments to smaller predecessor segments.)

Let 𝒲 be the set of all pairs (A,R) such that A⊆ω and R well-orders A. This really is a set: it is a definable subset of ℘(ω)×℘(ω×ω). Put two members of 𝒲 in the same equivalence class when they are order-isomorphic, and let Ω=𝒲/≅. The quotient is a set by Separation and Replacement. For α,β∈Ω define α≺β if a representative of α is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of a representative of β. This is independent of the representatives. The comparison theorem shows that ≺ is a strict total order; transitivity follows by composing the relevant isomorphisms (an initial segment of an initial segment is an initial segment).

We verify that ≺ well-orders Ω. Let S⊆Ω be nonempty and fix σ∈S. If no member of S is below σ, then σ is the least member of S. Otherwise, represent σ by (A,R), and form

D={a∈A : [(A_{<a},R restricted to A_{<a})]∈S}.

The set D is nonempty, because every order type below σ is represented by a unique proper initial segment A_{<a}. Let a₀ be the R-least member of D and let τ be the order type of A_{<a₀}. Then τ∈S. No member of S can lie below τ: such a member would also lie below σ and would therefore be the type of A_{<a} for some a R a₀, contradicting the choice of a₀. Since ≺ is total, τ is the least member of S. Thus (Ω,≺) is a well-ordered set. Notice that choosing one σ from one given nonempty S is ordinary existential instantiation, not an application of the axiom of choice.

For β=[(A,R)]∈Ω, consider the principal initial segment Ω_{<β}={α∈Ω:α≺β}. The map

φ:A→Ω_{<β},    φ(a)=[(A_{<a},R restricted to A_{<a})],

is a bijection. It is onto by the definition of ≺ and the fact that every proper initial segment of a well-order is A_{<a} for a unique a. It is one-to-one because, if a R b, then A_{<a} is a proper initial segment of A_{<b}, and those two well-orders cannot be isomorphic. Moreover, a R b holds exactly when φ(a)≺φ(b), so φ is an order isomorphism. Consequently Ω_{<β} injects into ω, since it is in bijection with A⊆ω. Every proper initial segment I of Ω is principal: the nonempty complement Ω∖I has a least element β, and downward closure gives I=Ω_{<β}. Hence every proper initial segment of Ω is countable.

It remains to show that Ω itself is uncountable. Suppose, toward a contradiction, that there were an injection j:Ω→ω. Let B=j[Ω]⊆ω, and transport ≺ along j to a well-order Q on B; then j is an order isomorphism (Ω,≺)→(B,Q). Since (B,Q)∈𝒲, its order type β=[(B,Q)] is an element of Ω. By the order isomorphism φ just constructed, (B,Q) is order-isomorphic to Ω_{<β}. Composing these two isomorphisms would make Ω order-isomorphic to its proper initial segment Ω_{<β}, which is impossible by the first paragraph. Therefore Ω does not inject into ω and is uncountable.

Thus Ω is an uncountable well-ordered set all of whose proper initial segments are countable, as required. The construction and every step of the argument take place in ZF and use no choice principle.
